title: Ethics in AI Products Starts in the Feature Brief
summary: AI ethics is mostly product work: consent, data limits, fairness checks, real human review, honest explanations and harm metrics, plus the laws in force as of Nov 2026.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The demo goes well. The prototype reads a customer's support message, guesses what they want and drafts a reply that saves the agent a couple of minutes per ticket. People around the table are nodding. Then the PM asks a plain question: "Did the customer know their message would be used like this?"

Nobody is trying to kill the feature. The conversation just shifts. You stop talking about latency and prompt tweaks and start talking about what the product promises the people whose data runs through it. In most teams, that's what AI ethics looks like up close: a handful of ordinary product decisions, made early, that decide whether anyone should trust the thing after launch.

This post takes those decisions in the order they tend to come up: consent, data, fairness, human review, explanations and metrics. Along the way you'll see which laws already apply as of November 2026, because "we'll sort out compliance later" now comes with dates attached.

Consent means nobody is surprised

A user can click "I agree" on the terms of service and still be shocked by what happens to their data. A better test is expectation: before the system acts, could the person reasonably guess what it's about to do? If a hiring tool summarizes interview notes, the candidate shouldn't have to wonder whether an AI was involved. If your support product uses old conversations to improve its drafts, customers and agents should both know where that line is.

Lawmakers have landed in the same place. Vietnam's Law on Artificial Intelligence, in force since 1 March 2026, requires providers to tell users when they're interacting with an AI system and to put machine-readable markers on AI-generated audio, images and video. Systems that were already running get 12 months to comply (China Briefing's summary of the law). In the EU, Article 50 of the AI Act says AI systems that talk to people must tell them so, at the latest at the first interaction, unless it's already obvious to a reasonably well-informed person (Article 50). That article applies from 2 August 2026.

Take only the data the feature needs

AI work makes "more context is better" feel true, and for answer quality it sometimes is. Being useful still doesn't give a feature permission to read everything. A reply-drafting feature probably needs the current ticket, a little recent account history and the relevant policy doc. It doesn't need private notes on other tickets, full history exports or sensitive fields that never change the answer.

A tight boundary pays off for engineers too. There's less to leak, fewer inputs to test, and when an output goes wrong you have a short list of suspects. For the everyday version of this problem, see what to strip out before you paste a ticket into an AI tool.

Averages hide who gets hurt

A model can look great on the dashboard and still fail one group of people over and over. The classic example is Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru's Gender Shades study. They tested three commercial gender classifiers on a face dataset balanced by gender and skin type. Error rates reached 34.7% for darker-skinned women, while the worst result for lighter-skinned men was 0.8% (Gender Shades, 2018). One overall accuracy number would never show that gap. It only appeared because the researchers split the results by gender and skin type together.

Your product probably doesn't classify faces, but the pattern carries over. An intent classifier might handle standard Vietnamese fine and stumble on messages typed without diacritics, regional slang or a Vietnamese-English mix. A ranking model might serve big accounts well and do badly for small shops that barely show up in the training data. A few habits catch this early:

  • Slice your eval set by groups that matter to your users (language, region, account size, device), where doing so is legal and safe.
  • Read real failing examples, not only the aggregate score.
  • Ask what the output touches. A grammar suggestion and a decision about someone's loan, job or account access deserve very different levels of care.

The EU AI Act draws the same line: it lists areas like recruitment, credit scoring and access to essential services as high-risk (Annex III). Under the AI Omnibus amendment published in July 2026, those obligations now apply from 2 December 2027 instead of August 2026 (FPF's updated timeline). Extra time to prepare is nice. The checks themselves haven't gone anywhere. For building sliced evals in practice, this post on evaluating an LLM feature goes into detail.

A human in the loop needs time, context and authority

"A human reviews it" is easy to write in a spec. Making that review real is harder when the queue is long, the AI sounds sure of itself and the reviewer is scored on throughput. Busy people lean on automated suggestions. The AI Act names this directly: Article 14 asks that people overseeing a high-risk system stay aware of automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on the output, and that they can disregard, override or reverse the output, or stop the system (Article 14).

In product terms, a reviewer needs:

  • Enough context to disagree. Show the source data, not only the AI's summary of it.
  • Enough time for hard cases, which means routing them to their own queue instead of mixing them in with quick approvals.
  • Real authority to override, without the override counting against them.

Then match the review to the consequence. A suggested rewording in an internal note can get a glance. An account suspension, a fraud flag or a rejected job application needs a named person who reads the case properly. For the reviewer's own habits, see using AI without handing over your judgment.

Explanations people can push back on

"Our system made this decision" protects the company more than it helps the person on the other end. A useful explanation says what happened, which information mattered and what the person can do next: correct their data, ask for a human, or appeal. Google's People + AI Guidebook treats this as design work. Its chapter on explainability and trust argues that users shouldn't trust an AI system in every situation, and that the goal is for their trust to match what the system can and can't do (Explainability + Trust).

A quick check: show your explanation text to someone outside the team and ask, "If you thought this was wrong, what would you do?" If they can't answer, the explanation isn't done yet.

Watch what the dashboard rewards

The strongest pressure on an AI feature usually comes from its metrics. A team can write careful principles and still ship something harmful if the dashboard only celebrates automation rate, cost per ticket or conversion. Score reviewers on throughput and they'll approve AI suggestions faster. Score the product on conversion and the predictions will drift toward nudging people into choices they wouldn't make with the full picture.

Next to each success metric, put at least one that would show harm: override rate, appeal rate, complaints per thousand decisions, error rate per user group. If the success number and the harm number climb together, you've learned something the success number would never have told you.

Write it into the feature brief

You don't need an ethics committee to start. You need a few extra lines in the brief you already write:

Six lines for the brief

Data: what the feature reads, and what it deliberately skips. Disclosure: where in the UI users learn that AI is involved. Groups: who might see more errors, and how we'll check. Review: which outputs a person must confirm, and who that person is. Explanation: what users see when the AI decides something about them. Harm metric: the number that would tell us it's going wrong.

If your company wants something more formal, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework released in January 2023, with a generative AI profile added in July 2024. It groups the work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage (NIST AI RMF). As of November 2026, NIST says version 1.0 is being revised, so check the page for the current version before you build a process around it.

One last test before launch: run the feature through a bad week in your head. A user complains. A journalist asks how it works. A support agent has to explain one decision. A regulator asks what data you used. An engineer has to trace why one recommendation showed up. If the brief and the logs answer all five, you're in good shape. Whichever one you can't answer is the next thing to write down.

Try this week

  • Open the brief of one AI feature you're working on and add the six lines above.
  • Split your eval results by one user group you haven't checked yet, and read ten failing examples.
  • Find the spot in the UI where users learn AI is involved. If it takes you more than a minute, your users won't find it either.
  • Add one harm metric next to the main success metric on your dashboard.

If your team gets stuck at the review step, The Cost of Trusting a Fluent AI Answer looks at why confident output gets waved through so easily.

faqs.q: What are the main ethical risks in an AI product?
faqs.a: Most of them are product decisions: using data people didn't expect you to use, collecting more data than the feature needs, errors that land on one group of users more than others, human review that exists only on paper, explanations nobody can act on, and metrics that reward speed over care.

faqs.q: Do I have to tell users they are talking to an AI?
faqs.a: In many places, yes. Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which applies from 2 August 2026, requires AI systems that interact with people to disclose it unless it's already obvious. Vietnam's Law on Artificial Intelligence, in force since 1 March 2026, also requires providers to tell users when they're interacting with an AI system.

faqs.q: How do I check an AI feature for bias?
faqs.a: Split your evaluation results by groups that matter to your users, such as language, region, account size or device, where that's legal and safe, and read the failing examples in each group. An overall accuracy number can hide large gaps: the Gender Shades study found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women against a worst case of 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.

faqs.q: What makes human review of AI output meaningful?
faqs.a: The reviewer needs the source data and not only the AI's summary, time for hard cases, and real authority to override without being penalized for it. Match the depth of review to the consequence: a text suggestion can get a glance, while decisions about someone's account, loan or job need a named person who reads each case.
